svg.title: Ray time on the head and worker pods
svg.text: Ray on the head and workers: workflow, functions, line numbers and measured times

Code: ej-prj-i4-5 fa974f21e (no Ray dashboard, 0.2 s connect retry), Ray 2.56.1. One sky launch (run 2 of 6) on 6 pods on k8s/kind-skypilot, one echo. Clock times are seconds from the start of sky launch.
The letter beside a time says where it comes from. Time ranges cover the 5 worker pods. The timeline is at the bottom.
timers in each Python process, in the trace image
timestamps in Ray's own logs: gcs_server.out, raylet.out, the agents' logs
Ray event stats, earlier sky exec trace (20261104-ray-api-trace)
ray start, GCS, raylet, agents; no dashboard
ray start, raylet, per-job Ray workers
Almost all Python start and imports for the ray CLI. GCS itself takes
tens of ms. Workers wait for this port.
No dashboard to wait for: start_api_server returns at once, so ray start
goes straight on to the raylet. With the dashboard this was 2.4–2.6 s.
Raylet waits for its two agents → registered
Both agents are now mostly Python start and imports. The runtime env
Now on the critical path: it sets when the Ray wait begins. With the
offline wheel install, runtime setup was 1.7–2.5 s across 6 launches: no
Set by the head's imports. ray start begins within 0.08 s of GCS
Poll for the head's node record
Now short: the head registers about 1.5 s after GCS starts, so most
workers find it on the first or second poll (1 median).
Raylet: connect to its own plasma store
The first connect still races the store thread and fails on 1 of 5
workers here (15 of 36 raylets in 6 launches), but the retry now comes
Raylet waits for its two agents → registered
No modules to load now: both agents are Python start and imports.
Skylet start, and wait for all 6 nodes
These run together, and the launch waits for both. Ray is now nearly
ready when the wait starts: it took 0.50 s (median), 1.83 s with the 1 s
Setup between Ray and the job
SkyPilot, not Ray: two Python commands on the head, mostly imports. Now
the largest gap before the job. Times per step are from the v2 trace;
home directory echo, rsync job script
Largest fixed cost in the job: import sky loads the whole backend,
though the driver uses five modules.

GCS asks each raylet to reserve

Includes importing what the task function needs.
After the last Ray call: Ray's shutdown and Python's exit, not broken

File mounts start → runtime setup end

Six sky launch runs on 6 pods, code ej-prj-i4-5 fa974f21e: 0.2 s head-node poll, lean skylet launcher, offline wheel install, no Ray dashboard, and 0.2 s local connect retries. Ray 2.56.1, kind on one machine,
so all pods share a clock. Wall times were 25.2, 23.5, 24.0, 22.0, 22.9, 24.0 s. The timeline is one real launch; the table shows how much each stage varies. There is no significance test here.

Against the v3 trace (1 s retry, same harness, another session), medians of 6 launches: GCS listening → last worker registered 3.48 → 3.02 s, alive-nodes wait 1.83 → 0.50 s, driver start 16.08 → 15.99 s, wall

23.60 → 23.73 s. The driver doesn't start sooner because the Ray wait now ends soon after it starts: the provisioner's file mounts and runtime setup before it, and SkyPilot's job setup after it, set the launch.
The C++ retry sleep isn't traced directly: raylet.out brackets it, from "Starting object store" to "ObjectManager server started" (about 3 ms without a retry). Every raylet's environment had both
RAY_raylet_client settings. The trace image adds timers to every Python process. Never benchmark latency with it.
